title: Offline EMS Reference Pack
disclaimer: Educational reference only. Protocols, scope, medication use, normal ranges, and equipment practices vary. Follow your agency, medical director, course, and current local protocols. Do not use this pack as the sole basis for patient care.

items.summary: Medical gas used to correct suspected or confirmed hypoxemia and support critically ill patients.
items.details: Indications depend on patient condition and local protocol. Titrate when appropriate; avoid delaying ventilation or airway management.
items.remember: Delivery device, flow, target saturation, response, fire risk.

items.summary: Antiplatelet medication commonly used for suspected acute coronary syndrome.
items.details: Confirm indications and contraindications; consider allergy, active bleeding, and local protocol.
items.remember: Chewable form, reassessment, bleeding risk.

items.summary: Vasodilator used in selected chest-pain and pulmonary-edema patients.
items.details: Check blood pressure, prescribed use when applicable, recent PDE-5 inhibitor use, and protocol.
items.remember: Hypotension, headache, repeat BP, symptom response.

items.summary: Short-acting bronchodilator for bronchospasm.
items.details: Assess breath sounds, work of breathing, heart rate, and ability to use the delivery device.
items.remember: Tremor, tachycardia, response to treatment.

items.summary: Anticholinergic bronchodilator often paired with albuterol in obstructive airway disease.
items.details: Used according to local protocol, commonly for asthma or COPD exacerbation.
items.remember: Dry mouth, delivery method, reassessment.

items.summary: Adrenergic medication used for severe allergic reactions and anaphylaxis.
items.details: Recognize airway swelling, breathing difficulty, shock, or rapidly progressing symptoms.
items.remember: Correct device/site, immediate transport, repeat assessment.

items.summary: Opioid antagonist used when opioid toxicity causes respiratory depression.
items.details: Ventilation remains the priority. Use according to protocol and reassess for recurrent respiratory depression.
items.remember: Airway, breathing, withdrawal, scene safety.

items.summary: Carbohydrate gel or paste used for selected conscious patients with suspected hypoglycemia.
items.details: Patient must be able to protect the airway and swallow. Follow glucose assessment and protocol.
items.remember: Aspiration risk, repeat glucose, symptom response.

items.summary: Hormone used for selected severe hypoglycemia when oral glucose is unsafe or ineffective.
items.details: Scope and route vary. Reassess airway, mental status, and glucose.
items.remember: Nausea/vomiting, delayed response, recovery position.

items.summary: Intravenous glucose used by appropriately credentialed clinicians for hypoglycemia.
items.details: Concentration and route vary by protocol. Confirm IV patency and reassess glucose.
items.remember: Extravasation, hyperglycemia, repeat assessment.

items.summary: Antiemetic used for nausea and vomiting.
items.details: Consider causes of vomiting, QT-risk factors, and local protocol.
items.remember: Route, response, ongoing hydration/transport needs.

items.summary: Analgesic and antipyretic used in selected systems.
items.details: Check total recent intake, liver risk, age/weight requirements, and protocol.
items.remember: Duplicate products, maximum daily exposure.

items.summary: NSAID used for pain or fever in selected systems.
items.details: Consider allergy, bleeding, kidney disease, pregnancy, and age restrictions.
items.remember: GI upset, hydration status, duplicate NSAID use.

items.summary: Antihistamine used in selected allergic reactions.
items.details: It does not replace epinephrine in anaphylaxis. Scope and route vary.
items.remember: Sedation, anticholinergic effects, airway monitoring.

items.summary: Adsorbent used rarely for selected ingestions under medical direction.
items.details: Not for caustics, hydrocarbons, altered patients without protected airway, or many other exposures.
items.remember: Poison-center/medical-control direction, aspiration risk.

items.summary: Isotonic crystalloid used for vascular access, medication delivery, and selected volume needs.
items.details: Amount and indication vary by patient and protocol.
items.remember: Lung sounds, perfusion, reassessment, fluid overload.

items.summary: Balanced crystalloid used in selected systems for fluid replacement.
items.details: Follow protocol and consider patient condition and compatibility.
items.remember: Perfusion, lung sounds, reassessment.

items.summary: Concentrated epinephrine formulation used for selected IM indications by authorized clinicians.
items.details: Concentration errors are dangerous. Verify indication, route, and formulation.
items.remember: Read label aloud, cross-check concentration.

items.summary: Dilute epinephrine formulation used for selected resuscitation indications by authorized clinicians.
items.details: Do not confuse with 1 mg/mL. Follow resuscitation protocol.
items.remember: Concentration, route, timing, documentation.

items.summary: Antiarrhythmic used in selected ventricular dysrhythmias by ALS clinicians.
items.details: Indication, rhythm, route, and sequence are protocol-specific.
items.remember: Rhythm, blood pressure, IV access, reassessment.

items.summary: Short-acting antiarrhythmic used for selected regular narrow-complex tachycardias.
items.details: Requires rhythm interpretation, rapid administration, monitoring, and protocol.
items.remember: Transient pause, patient explanation, rhythm strip.

items.summary: Anticholinergic used for selected symptomatic bradycardia and other indications.
items.details: Use depends on rhythm, symptoms, and protocol.
items.remember: Heart rate, perfusion, pacing readiness.

items.summary: Opioid analgesic used by authorized clinicians.
items.details: Assess pain, respiratory status, blood pressure, allergies, and protocol.
items.remember: Sedation, ventilation, reassessment.

items.summary: Dissociative medication used in selected systems for analgesia, sedation, or behavioral emergencies.
items.details: Indication and dosing vary greatly. Requires monitoring and airway readiness.
items.remember: Airway, emergence reactions, blood pressure.

items.summary: Benzodiazepine used for seizures, sedation, and selected agitation protocols.
items.details: Monitor ventilation and hemodynamics. Scope and route vary.
items.remember: Respiratory depression, sedation, reassessment.

items.summary: Medication used for selected dysrhythmias, severe asthma, or obstetric emergencies.
items.details: Indication and route are protocol-specific.
items.remember: Blood pressure, reflexes/respirations when relevant.

items.summary: Used for selected toxicologic, electrolyte, and resuscitation situations.
items.details: Formulation and compatibility matter. Follow protocol.
items.remember: IV patency, rhythm, medication compatibility.

items.summary: Alkalinizing medication used in selected toxicologic and resuscitation situations.
items.details: Not a routine medication for all arrests. Follow protocol.
items.remember: Ventilation, indication, IV compatibility.

items.summary: Commonly taught reference: 60-100 beats/min.
items.details: Interpret with symptoms, perfusion, medications, fitness, temperature, and trend.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Commonly taught reference: 12-20 breaths/min.
items.details: Count quality and effort, not only rate. Avoid announcing the count.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Often 95-100% in healthy adults at sea level.
items.details: Baseline, altitude, chronic lung disease, waveform quality, and clinical appearance matter.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: A single “normal” number is less useful than perfusion and trend. Many courses use about 90-120 mmHg as a basic reference.
items.details: Check cuff size, position, repeated readings, and symptoms.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: About 97-99°F (36.1-37.2°C) is a common oral reference range.
items.details: Route, environment, age, and device affect readings.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 100-180/min.
items.details: Use age-specific references from your course and protocol.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 100-160/min.
items.details: Assess perfusion and respiratory status; ranges vary with activity.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 90-150/min.
items.details: Crying and fever can increase rate.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 80-140/min.
items.details: Trend and appearance matter more than one isolated number.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 70-120/min.
items.details: Use local pediatric reference tools.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 60-100/min.
items.details: Approaches adult ranges.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 30-60/min.
items.details: Watch chest/abdomen, effort, color, and pauses.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 30-50/min.
items.details: Count a full minute when irregular.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 24-40/min.
items.details: Observe before touching when possible.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 22-34/min.
items.details: Retractions, grunting, and nasal flaring are important.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 18-30/min.
items.details: Consider fever, anxiety, pain, and exertion.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Common EMS teaching range: roughly 12-20/min.
items.details: Interpret similarly to adults while considering age.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: Often less than 2 seconds in a warm, well-perfused patient.
items.details: Cold, age, lighting, and technique affect the result.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: A commonly taught adult reference is about 35-45 mmHg.
items.details: Interpret waveform, ventilation, perfusion, clinical context, and trend.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.

items.summary: A common fasting laboratory reference is about 70-99 mg/dL, but EMS interpretation depends on symptoms, meal timing, diabetes, and protocol.
items.details: Treat the patient and follow local thresholds.
items.remember: Ranges are teaching references, not universal treatment thresholds.
